newsitem.title: USA: U.S. man to be executed despite papal plea.
newsitem.headline: U.S. man to be executed despite papal plea.

text.p: Virginia authorities say they intend to go ahead with the execution on Wednesday of convicted murderer Joseph Roger O'Dell despite appeals from Pope John Paul and Italian authorities for clemency.

Although a clemency petition is before Governor George Allen, prison officials were moving ahead with preparations for the execution, said David Botkins, a spokesman for the Virginia Department of Corrections.

O'Dell is due to die by lethal injection on Wednesday at 9 p.m. EDT (0100 GMT Thursday) for the 1985 rape and murder of Helen Schartner of Virginia Beach, Virginia. Police said he abducted, pistol-whipped, raped and strangled the 44-year-old secretary before dumping her body in a field.
O'Dell was arrested after leaving bloody clothing at a girlfriend's house. She turned him in after learning the slaying had occurred in an area that O'Dell frequented.
The case was one of the costliest in Virginia history by the time of his 1986 conviction. But it has since become possibly the most contentious capital murder case in the state's history.
And, although he has no ties to Italy, O'Dell has become a cause celebre there.

Pope John Paul and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi have led a chorus of protest against his death sentence. On Monday alone, the Vatican's television station made a plea for clemency and Prodi told reporters in Luxemburg he had made "a last, very strong, heartfelt appeal" to Allen.
Italian officials met Allen's counsel Mark Christie on Monday and asked him to permit a new DNA test.
"I think nobody can say that he is sure Joseph O'Dell is guilty," said Leoluca Orlando, mayor of Palermo and a member of the European Parliament. "I hope that Governor Allen will stop this execution.
Allen, a Republican known for his vigorous anti-crime stance, said he believes O'Dell is guilty and refused to allow new DNA testing in the case.

The condemned man's supporters questioned the testing. A DNA test done on O'Dell's shirt in 1990 showed that blood on it did not belong to O'Dell or Schartner. But tests on the blood on his jacket showed by odds of 166,000 to one that the blood was Schartner's.
The National Coalition to Abolish the Death Penalty urged Allen to allow DNA testing of a sperm sample.

The coalition's director, Steve Hawkins, told a news conference on Tuesday O'Dell's case "underscores for us many of the problems that we see inherent in the use of the death penalty in the United States."
The case was one where new scientific advances may be able to prove innocence, he said. "We feel quiet strongly that he is richly deserving of a reprieve from the governor."

O'Dell is represented by Washington and New York law firms as well as a New York public relations agency. His "spiritual adviser" is Sister Helen Prejean, author of "Dead Man Walking," the best-selling book that was made into a movie.
Lori Urs, a paralegal who is a close friend of O'Dell, said she had met with him for an hour on Monday and that he was holding up well.
"Joe has faith, continues to hope and pray that the governor will grant him a reprieve," she said.
But Schartner's sister, Gail Lee of Virginia Beach, said the family was weary of the long process.
"We're surviving (though) it's getting a little rough," she said, recounting telephone calls from Italian journalists.
There were eight executions in Virginia in 1996. This year, three people have been put to death in the state.
O'Dell's execution had been scheduled for Dec. 18, 1996, but was stayed that day by the U.S. Supreme Court.
